heading: O1 - Multi-agent architecture, orchestration, uncertainty hand-off and audit trail

papers.title: MDAgents: An Adaptive Collaboration of LLMs for Medical Decision-Making
papers.authors: Kim Y, Park C, Jeong H, Chan YS, Xu X, McDuff D, Lee H, Ghassemi M, Breazeal C, Park HW
papers.aim: To let LLM agents decide how much teamwork a medical question really needs, instead of fixing one setup for every case.
papers.method: A moderator agent first rates the case complexity. Easy cases go to one doctor agent, medium cases go to a multi-disciplinary team that discusses, and hard cases go to an integrated care team that writes a final report.
papers.result: Best accuracy on 7 of 10 medical benchmarks (MedQA, PMC-VQA, Path-VQA etc). Adding moderator review and external medical knowledge gave a further clear gain.
papers.tools: GPT-4 / GPT-4V, Gemini-Pro, prompt engineering, role-play agents, majority voting
papers.gap: Only question-answer benchmarks. No real patient pathway, no calibrated confidence, and the human doctor is not part of the loop.
papers.relation: Same idea as our orchestrator that routes tasks. But they route by question difficulty, we want to route by measured uncertainty and send hard cases to a real clinician.
papers.limitations: High API cost, LLM hallucination, and results come from public QA sets, not hospital data. Future: real clinical data and human review.

papers.title: MedAgents: Large Language Models as Collaborators for Zero-shot Medical Reasoning
papers.authors: Tang X, Zou A, Zhang Z, Li Z, Zhao Y, Zhang X, Cohan A, Gerstein M
papers.aim: To improve medical reasoning of LLMs without any training, by making several LLM 'experts' discuss a case.
papers.method: Five steps: gather domain experts, each expert writes analysis, summarise into a report, experts discuss and vote until agreement, then final decision.
papers.result: Beat zero-shot chain-of-thought and self-consistency on MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA and medical parts of MMLU.
papers.tools: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, role-playing prompts, consensus voting
papers.gap: Errors still come from missing domain knowledge and wrong retrieval. Text only, multiple-choice questions only.
papers.relation: Supports our design of specialised agents (MRI, pathology, diagnosis). Gives a simple way to resolve disagreement between agents before escalation.
papers.limitations: No uncertainty value, no audit log, no image input. Future work they mention: better knowledge grounding.

papers.title: Agent Hospital: A Simulacrum of Hospital with Evolvable Medical Agents
papers.authors: Li J, Wang S, Zhang M, Li W, Lai Y, Kang X, Ma W, Liu Y
papers.aim: To build a simulated hospital where patient, nurse and doctor agents interact, so doctor agents can improve from cases without labelled data.
papers.method: Whole hospital flow is simulated (triage, registration, consultation, exam, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up). Doctor agents use MedAgent-Zero, storing successful cases and lessons from failures.
papers.result: After treating a very large number of simulated patients, doctor agents reported about 93% accuracy on a respiratory subset of MedQA.
papers.tools: LLM agents (GPT-3.5/GPT-4), memory / experience base, simulated environment
papers.gap: All simulated. Not tested with real clinicians or real patients. Simulated patients may be too simple.
papers.relation: Their hospital flow is close to our pathway (intake, MRI, pathology, diagnosis, surgery planning, follow-up). Idea: we can test our orchestrator in a simulated pathway before using registry data.
papers.limitations: Simulation bias, no safety check, no human validation step. Future: link with real hospital systems.

papers.title: AgentClinic: a multimodal agent benchmark to evaluate AI in simulated clinical environments
papers.authors: Schmidgall S, Ziaei R, Harris C, Reis E, Jopling J, Moor M
papers.aim: To test LLM doctors in an interactive, step-by-step clinical setting instead of static exam questions.
papers.method: Doctor agent must take history, order tests from a measurement agent and give diagnosis. Patient agents can carry cognitive and demographic biases. Includes image cases from NEJM.
papers.result: Models that score high on MedQA lose a lot of accuracy in the sequential setting. Bias and tool use change results noticeably.
papers.tools: Multiple LLMs (GPT-4, Claude, Llama etc), multimodal LLMs, simulated patients
papers.gap: Still simulated dialogue. Diagnosis only, no treatment or surgical step.
papers.relation: Good evidence that static accuracy is misleading, which supports our O4 argument. Their sequential test setup can be used to stress-test our agent chain.
papers.limitations: Synthetic cases, limited images. Future: more specialties and real clinical evaluation.

papers.title: Development and validation of an autonomous artificial intelligence agent for clinical decision-making in oncology
papers.authors: Ferber D, El Nahhas OSM, Wolflein G, Wiest IC, Clusmann J, et al., Kather JN
papers.aim: To check if an LLM that can call specialised oncology tools can make better clinical decisions than the LLM alone.
papers.method: GPT-4 acts as the central agent and calls tools: vision transformers for mutation prediction from histology, MedSAM for radiology segmentation, OncoKB, PubMed search, and retrieval from oncology guidelines. Tested on 20 realistic multimodal patient cases.
papers.result: Decision accuracy went from about 30% (GPT-4 alone) to about 87% with tools. Most tool calls were correct and most answers cited guidelines.
papers.tools: GPT-4, RAG over guidelines, vision transformers, MedSAM, OncoKB API, PubMed
papers.gap: Only 20 cases, not prospective, no deferral rule. Errors in one tool can flow silently to the final answer.
papers.relation: Closest design to ours: an orchestrator + imaging tool + pathology tool. Our extra contribution is passing uncertainty between tools and forcing clinician check when confidence is low.
papers.limitations: Small evaluation set, GPT-4 dependency, privacy issue with cloud LLM. Future: larger validation, local models.

papers.title: MMedAgent: Learning to Use Medical Tools with Multi-modal Agent
papers.authors: Li B, Yan T, Pan Y, Luo J, Ji R, Ding J, Xu Z, Liu S, Dong H, Lin Z, Wang Y
papers.aim: To build one multimodal medical agent that learns which tool to call for a given image task.
papers.method: Instruction-tuned LLaVA-Med on a tool-use dataset. Tools cover grounding, segmentation, classification, report generation and retrieval across several imaging modalities.
papers.result: Did better than open-source medical models and GPT-4o on most tested tasks, and new tools can be added easily.
papers.tools: LLaVA-Med, MedSAM, Grounding DINO, BiomedCLIP, instruction tuning
papers.gap: Tool choice is learned but there is no confidence check on tool outputs.
papers.relation: Shows a trained router is possible. Our MRI agent and pathology agent could be called the same way, but we add uncertainty to each call.
papers.limitations: Fixed tool list, mostly 2D images, not brain MRI volumes. Future: more tools and modalities.

papers.title: AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation
papers.authors: Wu Q, Bansal G, Zhang J, Wu Y, Li B, Zhu E, Jiang L, Zhang X, Zhang S, Liu J, Awadallah AH, White RW, Burger D, Wang C
papers.aim: To give a general open-source framework for building applications from several agents that talk to each other.
papers.method: 'Conversable' agents that can be LLMs, tools or humans. Developer defines the conversation pattern. A human proxy agent can ask a person for input at set points.
papers.result: Worked on maths, retrieval QA, coding, decision making tasks and reduced the coding effort to build multi-agent systems.
papers.tools: Python, OpenAI LLMs, tool execution, human-input modes
papers.gap: Not designed for safety-critical use. No standard way of logging decisions for audit.
papers.relation: Possible implementation framework for our prototype. The human proxy agent maps nicely to our clinician validation point.
papers.limitations: Chat-based state is hard to verify. Future: better control flow and evaluation tools.

papers.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
papers.authors: Yao S, Zhao J, Yu D, Du N, Shafran I, Narasimhan K, Cao Y
papers.aim: To make LLMs think and take actions (use tools) in the same loop.
papers.method: Model writes a thought, takes an action (e.g. search), reads the observation, and repeats.
papers.result: Fewer hallucinations on HotpotQA and FEVER. On ALFWorld and WebShop it beat imitation and RL methods by a large margin (34% and 10% absolute).
papers.tools: PaLM, GPT-3, few-shot prompting, Wikipedia API
papers.gap: Long reasoning chains can still go wrong, and the model does not know when to stop and ask a human.
papers.relation: Basic loop for each of our agents. The thought-action-observation trace is useful as a readable record for the audit trail.
papers.limitations: Depends on prompt examples. Future: fine-tuning on more traces.

papers.title: A survey on large language model based autonomous agents
papers.authors: Wang L, Ma C, Feng X, Zhang Z, Yang H, Zhang J, et al., Wen JR
papers.aim: To review how LLM-based agents are built, used and evaluated.
papers.method: Literature review. They propose a common framework with profile, memory, planning and action modules.
papers.result: A clear taxonomy of agent design, applications (incl. science and medicine) and evaluation methods.
papers.gap: Safety, evaluation standards, and role reliability are listed as open problems.
papers.relation: Useful to describe our architecture in standard terms in the thesis (each agent = profile + memory + planning + action).
papers.limitations: Moves fast, some parts already outdated. Not medical specific.

papers.title: Model Cards for Model Reporting
papers.authors: Mitchell M, Wu S, Zaldivar A, Barnes P, Vasserman L, Hutchinson B, Spitzer E, Raji ID, Gebru T
papers.aim: To propose a short standard document that comes with every trained model.
papers.method: Defined sections: model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, training data, ethical points, caveats. Showed two example cards.
papers.result: Model cards became a widely used reporting practice.
papers.gap: It is static and voluntary. Nothing checks at runtime that the model is used inside its tested conditions.
papers.relation: Our proposal mentions a model-facts statement for each agent. Model cards give the template. We can extend it so the orchestrator checks it at runtime.
papers.limitations: Not medical. Future: automatic and living documentation.

papers.title: Closing the AI Accountability Gap: Defining an End-to-End Framework for Internal Algorithmic Auditing
papers.authors: Raji ID, Smart A, White RN, Mitchell M, Gebru T, Hutchinson B, Smith-Loud J, Theron D, Barnes P
papers.aim: To define how an organisation can audit its own AI system from start to end.
papers.method: SMACTR framework: Scoping, Mapping, Artifact collection, Testing, Reflection, with documents produced at each stage.
papers.result: A practical audit process and list of audit artifacts.
papers.gap: Organisational process only, no technical logging design.
papers.relation: Helps us decide what our audit record must hold so a reviewer can rebuild who decided what and why.
papers.limitations: Not tested in hospitals. Future: link to regulation.

papers.title: Towards Conversational Diagnostic AI (AMIE)
papers.authors: Tu T, Palepu A, Schaekermann M, Saab K, Freyberg J, et al., Natarajan V
papers.aim: To build an LLM that can take a medical history and give a diagnosis through conversation.
papers.method: Self-play training in a simulated environment with automatic feedback. Tested in a blinded OSCE-style study with patient actors against primary care doctors.
papers.result: Higher diagnostic accuracy than the doctors and rated better on most quality axes by specialists and by patient actors.
papers.tools: PaLM-2 based LLM, self-play, simulated dialogue
papers.gap: Text chat only, which is not how real consultations happen. Not tested in real practice.
papers.relation: Relevant to our patient-intake agent. Their OSCE-style blinded evaluation can be adapted for O4.
papers.limitations: Chat setting unfair to doctors, no images. Future: real-world studies.

heading: O2 - Calibrated uncertainty and escalation (when to defer to the clinician)

papers.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
papers.authors: Guo C, Pleiss G, Sun Y, Weinberger KQ
papers.aim: To check if the confidence scores of modern deep networks match their real accuracy.
papers.method: Measured calibration with ECE and reliability diagrams on many networks and datasets. Compared post-hoc fixes.
papers.result: Modern deep networks are over-confident. Depth, width, batch norm and less weight decay make it worse. Temperature scaling (one parameter) fixes most of it.
papers.tools: ResNet, DenseNet, Wide-ResNet; CIFAR, ImageNet, text datasets
papers.gap: Only tested on the same distribution as training.
papers.relation: Every agent in our system must be calibrated before we use its confidence for escalation. Temperature scaling is our first baseline.
papers.limitations: Calibration breaks when data shifts (new hospital). Future: shift-robust calibration.

papers.title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
papers.authors: Gal Y, Ghahramani Z
papers.aim: To get model uncertainty from normal deep networks without changing them much.
papers.method: Showed dropout training is approximate Bayesian inference. Keep dropout on at test time and run many forward passes (MC dropout).
papers.result: Better predictive log-likelihood and RMSE on regression tasks, and useful uncertainty in classification and RL.
papers.gap: Uncertainty quality depends on dropout rate, and is often still too low.
papers.relation: Cheap way to get epistemic uncertainty for our MRI segmentation and classification agents on modest hardware.
papers.limitations: Several forward passes needed, so slower at inference. Future: better approximations.

papers.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
papers.authors: Lakshminarayanan B, Pritzel A, Blundell C
papers.aim: To give a simple, non-Bayesian way to estimate predictive uncertainty.
papers.method: Train several networks with different random starts, using proper scoring rules (and optional adversarial training), then average.
papers.result: Well-calibrated predictions and higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution samples, often better than MC dropout.
papers.gap: Training and running many models costs a lot.
papers.relation: Strong UQ baseline to compare with MC dropout for our agents. Cost matters in low-resource hospitals.
papers.limitations: Compute and memory cost. Future: lighter ensembles.

papers.title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
papers.authors: Geifman Y, El-Yaniv R
papers.aim: To let a network refuse to predict on uncertain inputs while guaranteeing a chosen error rate.
papers.method: Selection with Guaranteed Risk (SGR): pick a confidence threshold on held-out data so the error on accepted cases stays under a target, with high probability. Tested softmax response and MC dropout.
papers.result: On ImageNet they could guarantee 2% top-5 error while still covering about 60% of images.
papers.gap: Single model, single decision, same cost for every mistake.
papers.relation: The risk-coverage trade-off is basically our escalation threshold. We need to extend it to asymmetric error cost and to a chain of agents.
papers.limitations: Guarantee assumes test data like calibration data. Future: training models for selection.

papers.title: Consistent Estimators for Learning to Defer to an Expert
papers.authors: Mozannar H, Sontag D
papers.aim: To train a classifier and a 'defer to the expert' decision together, with a sound loss.
papers.method: Adds an extra 'defer' class and a consistent surrogate loss based on cross-entropy, taking expert accuracy into account.
papers.result: Beat confidence-based and earlier L2D baselines on CIFAR-10 with synthetic experts, CIFAR-100, CheXpert and hate-speech data.
papers.gap: Needs expert labels on training data. Does not limit how many cases go to the expert.
papers.relation: Core method for O2. We need to add the limit of clinician review time and the clinical cost of each error type.
papers.limitations: One expert, one decision. Future: multiple experts and budget constraints.

papers.title: Predict Responsibly: Improving Fairness and Accuracy by Learning to Defer
papers.authors: Madras D, Pitassi T, Zemel R
papers.aim: To show that a model should defer by thinking about who will receive the case, not only its own confidence.
papers.method: Learning-to-defer model that is trained with the downstream decision maker in mind, compared with simple reject option.
papers.result: Better accuracy and fairness of the whole system on COMPAS and Heritage Health data.
papers.gap: Decision makers were simulated.
papers.relation: Supports our idea that deferral depends on the clinician (radiologist, pathologist, neurosurgeon) who will review it.
papers.limitations: Not tested in medicine. Future: real human decision makers.

papers.title: The Algorithmic Automation Problem: Prediction, Triage, and Human Effort
papers.authors: Raghu M, Blumer K, Corrado G, Kleinberg J, Obermeyer Z, Mullainathan S
papers.aim: To decide which cases an algorithm should handle and which should go to humans, to use human effort well.
papers.method: Triage using predicted human error / disagreement plus model uncertainty. Tested on medical data like diabetic retinopathy grading.
papers.result: Mixing algorithm and human by triage did better than full automation or full human review.
papers.gap: Workflow and time cost of humans not modelled in detail.
papers.relation: Our case: specialist time is the scarcest thing. This paper frames the problem in the same way.
papers.limitations: Preprint, retrospective only. Future: prospective test.

papers.title: Enhancing the reliability and accuracy of AI-enabled diagnosis via complementarity-driven deferral to clinicians (CoDoC)
papers.authors: Dvijotham K, Winkens J, Barsbey M, et al., Karthikesalingam A
papers.aim: To learn when to trust a predictive AI and when to defer to the clinician, in real screening.
papers.method: CoDoC uses only the AI confidence score, the clinician's read and ground truth from past data to learn deferral regions. Does not need access to the model inside.
papers.result: In breast cancer screening data it cut false positives (around 25% in the UK set) at the same false negatives and reduced clinician workload a lot. Also tested on TB screening.
papers.tools: Density estimation on confidence scores, mammography and chest X-ray AI
papers.gap: Single AI model and single decision. Retrospective.
papers.relation: The closest prior work to our O2. Our difference: a chain of agents, brain MRI + pathology, and small Sri Lankan data.
papers.limitations: Needs enough labelled past cases with clinician opinion. Future: prospective use.
papers.pdf: Not downloaded - get from link / library

papers.title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification
papers.authors: Angelopoulos AN, Bates S
papers.aim: To explain conformal prediction in a practical way.
papers.method: Tutorial with code: split conformal, adaptive sets, conformal risk control, examples on images and medicine.
papers.result: Shows how to turn any model output into prediction sets with a guaranteed coverage.
papers.gap: Guarantee needs exchangeable data, which is not true across hospitals.
papers.relation: For tumour type we can give a set of likely classes with a coverage guarantee. A large set = escalate. Works with small calibration sets.
papers.limitations: Coverage only on average, not per patient. Future: shift-aware conformal.

papers.title: Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
papers.authors: Ovadia Y, Fertig E, Ren J, Nado Z, Sculley D, Nowozin S, Dillon JV, Lakshminarayanan B, Snoek J
papers.aim: To compare uncertainty methods when test data is shifted from training data.
papers.method: Large benchmark of methods (vanilla, temperature scaling, dropout, ensembles, SVI, last-layer) under increasing shift and OOD data.
papers.result: Calibration gets worse as shift grows. Temperature scaling on clean validation does not hold. Deep ensembles were the most robust.
papers.gap: No method was good under strong shift.
papers.relation: Sri Lankan scanners and protocols are a dataset shift from BraTS. We must test calibration on local data, not just public data.
papers.limitations: Not medical imaging. Future: shift-robust methods.

papers.title: Confidence Calibration and Predictive Uncertainty Estimation for Deep Medical Image Segmentation
papers.authors: Mehrtash A, Wells WM, Tempany CM, Abolmaesumi P, Kapur T
papers.aim: To study calibration and uncertainty of segmentation networks in medical images.
papers.method: Compared Dice vs cross-entropy loss, model ensembles, and proposed segment-level uncertainty. Datasets incl. prostate, heart and brain tumour MRI.
papers.result: Dice-trained models are badly calibrated. Ensembles improve calibration. Segment-level uncertainty relates to how good the Dice is, so it can flag bad segmentations.
papers.tools: FCN / U-Net style models, ensembles, MRI
papers.gap: Ensembles are costly, and no link to a decision (accept or refer).
papers.relation: Direct use in our MRI agent: give a per-tumour uncertainty that is passed to the next agent and used for escalation.
papers.limitations: Few datasets. Future: cheaper UQ.

papers.title: QU-BraTS: MICCAI BraTS 2020 Challenge on Quantifying Uncertainty in Brain Tumor Segmentation
papers.authors: Mehta R, Filos A, Baid U, Sako C, McKinley R, Rebsamen M, et al., Arbel T
papers.aim: To create a fair way to score uncertainty maps in brain tumour segmentation and compare methods.
papers.method: New score that rewards confidence on correct voxels and uncertainty on wrong ones, and penalises throwing away too many correct voxels. Used to rank challenge teams.
papers.result: Ranked many teams. Ensemble and test-time augmentation methods were common among top teams.
papers.tools: BraTS 2020 multi-parametric MRI, 3D CNNs, ensembles, TTA
papers.gap: Voxel-level score only, not linked to clinical decisions.
papers.relation: Ready-made metric to evaluate our MRI agent uncertainty in a brain tumour setting.
papers.limitations: Only BraTS (adult glioma) data. Future: link uncertainty to clinical use.

papers.title: Second opinion needed: communicating uncertainty in medical machine learning
papers.authors: Kompa B, Snoek J, Beam AL
papers.aim: To argue why medical ML must show uncertainty and be able to say 'I don't know'.
papers.method: Perspective paper with examples and overview of UQ methods.
papers.result: Recommends that models abstain when uncertain and that uncertainty is reported in medical ML studies.
papers.gap: No new method or experiment.
papers.relation: Good motivation reference for our problem statement and O2.
papers.limitations: Opinion piece. Future: standards for reporting uncertainty.

heading: O3 - Data-efficient MRI and pathology models, fusion and federated learning

papers.title: nnU-Net: a self-configuring method for deep learning-based biomedical image segmentation
papers.authors: Isensee F, Jaeger PF, Kohl SAA, Petersen J, Maier-Hein KH
papers.aim: To make segmentation work out-of-the-box on any new medical dataset without manual tuning.
papers.method: Rules that set preprocessing, network (2D/3D U-Net), training and post-processing automatically from dataset properties.
papers.result: Beat most specialised methods on 23 public datasets and many challenges.
papers.gap: Needs strong GPU and no uncertainty output by default.
papers.relation: Our main baseline for tumour segmentation on Sri Lankan MRI.
papers.limitations: Heavy compute, still needs good labels. Future: lighter and label-efficient versions.

papers.title: The RSNA-ASNR-MICCAI BraTS 2021 Benchmark on Brain Tumor Segmentation and Radiogenomic Classification
papers.authors: Baid U, Ghodasara S, Mohan S, Bilello M, Calabrese E, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To describe the BraTS 2021 dataset and tasks.
papers.method: Large multi-institution multi-parametric MRI (T1, T1Gd, T2, FLAIR) with expert labels for enhancing tumour, tumour core and whole tumour. Also MGMT prediction task.
papers.result: Around 2,000 glioma cases, the biggest public brain tumour MRI set at that time.
papers.tools: Multi-parametric MRI, standard preprocessing (skull strip, co-registration)
papers.gap: Mostly gliomas from Western centres, pre-processed and standardised.
papers.relation: Public pre-training and benchmark set before we use local data. Also shows the gap: our data is not standardised.
papers.limitations: Population and scanner bias. Future: more tumour types and regions.

papers.title: Swin UNETR: Swin Transformers for Semantic Segmentation of Brain Tumors in MRI Images
papers.authors: Hatamizadeh A, Nath V, Tang Y, Yang D, Roth HR, Xu D
papers.aim: To use a Swin transformer encoder for 3D brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: Swin transformer encoder with shifted windows, CNN decoder, skip connections. Trained on BraTS 2021.
papers.result: Among the top methods in BraTS 2021 validation.
papers.gap: Transformers usually need lots of data.
papers.relation: Candidate model for our MRI agent, compared with nnU-Net.
papers.limitations: Heavy model, small data risk. Future: pretraining.

papers.title: Self-Supervised Pre-Training of Swin Transformers for 3D Medical Image Analysis
papers.authors: Tang Y, Yang D, Li W, Roth HR, Landman B, Xu D, Nath V, Hatamizadeh A
papers.aim: To pretrain 3D models on unlabelled scans so less labelled data is needed later.
papers.method: Self-supervised tasks: masked volume inpainting, rotation prediction and contrastive coding, on about 5,000 unlabelled CT scans.
papers.result: State-of-the-art results on BTCV and Medical Segmentation Decathlon after fine-tuning.
papers.gap: Pretrained on CT, transfer to brain MRI not shown well.
papers.relation: Our labelled Sri Lankan data will be small. Self-supervised pretraining on unlabelled local MRI is a key option.
papers.limitations: Big compute for pretraining. Future: pretraining on MRI.

papers.title: Segment Anything in Medical Images (MedSAM)
papers.authors: Ma J, He Y, Li F, Han L, You C, Wang B
papers.aim: To build one promptable segmentation model for many medical image types.
papers.method: Fine-tuned Segment Anything on over 1.5 million medical image-mask pairs across 10 modalities. User gives a bounding box.
papers.result: Better than SAM and comparable or better than specialist models on many internal and external tests.
papers.gap: 2D slices, needs a box prompt, weaker on very small or unclear edges.
papers.relation: Clinician can draw a box and correct the result. Good for human-in-the-loop correction and fast labelling of local data.
papers.limitations: Not 3D native. Future: 3D and text prompts.

papers.title: Attention-based Deep Multiple Instance Learning
papers.authors: Ilse M, Tomczak JM, Welling M
papers.aim: To learn from bag-level labels only (e.g. one label per slide) and still find important instances.
papers.method: Attention pooling over instance features, trained end-to-end.
papers.result: Matched or beat other MIL methods and gives attention maps showing important patches (tested on histopathology data).
papers.gap: Assumes instances are independent.
papers.relation: Biopsy slides will have only slide-level diagnosis. This is the basic method for our pathology agent.
papers.limitations: Small datasets in paper. Future: larger WSI.

papers.title: Data-efficient and weakly supervised computational pathology on whole-slide images (CLAM)
papers.authors: Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Chen TY, Chen RJ, Barbieri M, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To classify whole slides using only slide labels and small datasets.
papers.method: Attention MIL with clustering constraint on top of frozen pretrained features. Tested on renal cancer subtyping, lung cancer subtyping and lymph node metastasis.
papers.result: High AUC with limited labels, worked on independent test sets and even on smartphone microscopy images. Gives interpretable heatmaps.
papers.tools: ResNet-50 features, attention MIL, PyTorch, OpenSlide
papers.gap: Not tested on brain tumours. Feature extractor from ImageNet.
papers.relation: Strong baseline for our pathology agent on small Sri Lankan biopsy sets.
papers.limitations: Scanner/stain differences. Future: better features.

papers.title: Towards a general-purpose foundation model for computational pathology (UNI)
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Ding T, Lu MY, Williamson DFK, Jaume G, et al., Mahmood F
papers.aim: To pretrain one strong pathology feature model useful for many tasks.
papers.method: Self-supervised (DINOv2) training on over 100 million tissue patches from about 100,000 slides, tested on 34 tasks.
papers.result: Better than earlier pathology encoders on most tasks, including rare cancer classification and few-shot learning.
papers.gap: Trained on US hospital data. Licence and compute limits.
papers.relation: Feature extractor for our pathology agent so we need fewer local labels.
papers.limitations: Bias to source data, big model. Future: multimodal.

papers.title: Pathomic Fusion: An Integrated Framework for Fusing Histopathology and Genomic Features for Cancer Diagnosis and Prognosis
papers.authors: Chen RJ, Lu MY, Wang J, Williamson DFK, Rodig SJ, Lindeman NI, Mahmood F
papers.aim: To combine histology images and molecular data for glioma grading and survival.
papers.method: CNN and graph network features from histology fused with genomic features using gated attention and Kronecker product.
papers.result: Fusion did better than single-source models and the WHO 2016 grading on TCGA glioma and kidney cancer.
papers.gap: Assumes all data sources are present for every patient.
papers.relation: Our combined diagnosis agent fuses imaging, pathology and lab markers. We need it to work when markers are missing.
papers.limitations: TCGA data only. Future: handle missing modalities.

papers.title: Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data (FedAvg)
papers.authors: McMahan HB, Moore E, Ramage D, Hampson S, Aguera y Arcas B
papers.aim: To train a shared model without collecting raw data in one place.
papers.method: Federated Averaging: each client trains locally for some steps, server averages the weights.
papers.result: Needed far fewer communication rounds than synchronised SGD, and worked with non-IID data in their tests.
papers.gap: Performance drops with strong data differences between clients.
papers.relation: The basic federation method we start with across hospitals.
papers.limitations: No privacy guarantee alone. Future: heterogeneity handling.

papers.title: Federated Optimization in Heterogeneous Networks (FedProx)
papers.authors: Li T, Sahu AK, Zaheer M, Sanjabi M, Talwalkar A, Smith V
papers.aim: To make federated training stable when clients have very different data and compute.
papers.method: Adds a proximal term so local models do not drift too far from the global model, and allows partial work from clients.
papers.result: More stable convergence and better accuracy than FedAvg in heterogeneous settings (around 22% average absolute gain in very heterogeneous settings).
papers.gap: Extra hyper-parameter to tune.
papers.relation: Our case is a few hospitals with small and very different cohorts. FedProx is a must-try baseline.
papers.limitations: Not medical data. Future: personalisation.

papers.title: FedBN: Federated Learning on Non-IID Features via Local Batch Normalization
papers.authors: Li X, Jiang M, Zhang X, Kamp M, Dou Q
papers.aim: To handle feature shift between clients, like different scanners.
papers.method: Keep batch normalisation layers local at each client and only average the other weights.
papers.result: Better than FedAvg and FedProx on feature-shift benchmarks, including a medical imaging one.
papers.gap: Only for models with BN, and a new site needs some local data.
papers.relation: Scanner and protocol differences between Sri Lankan hospitals are exactly this feature shift.
papers.limitations: Small number of clients tested. Future: other normalisation types.

papers.title: Federated learning in medicine: facilitating multi-institutional collaborations without sharing patient data
papers.authors: Sheller MJ, Edwards B, Reina GA, Martin J, Pati S, Kotrotsou A, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To check if federated learning can match central training for brain tumour segmentation.
papers.method: BraTS data split by institution, compared federated learning with institutional incremental and cyclic training, and with data-sharing.
papers.result: Federated model reached about 99% of the quality of the centrally trained model, better than the other collaborative methods.
papers.gap: Simulated federation on public data, not real hospitals.
papers.relation: Direct proof that FL works for brain tumour MRI. Our job is to show it with a few small real Sri Lankan sites.
papers.limitations: Simulated sites. Future: real deployment.

papers.title: Federated learning enables big data for rare cancer boundary detection
papers.authors: Pati S, Baid U, Edwards B, Sheller M, Wang SH, et al., Bakas S
papers.aim: To run a real worldwide federated study for glioblastoma boundary detection.
papers.method: 71 sites on 6 continents trained a segmentation model together with FL, data never left the site.
papers.result: Big improvement over the model trained on public data for both surgically targetable tumour and whole tumour boundaries.
papers.gap: Large sites with good IT. Little on what happens with a handful of small sites.
papers.relation: Biggest real FL proof in brain tumours. Our gap is small low-resource sites, which they did not study.
papers.limitations: Heterogeneity across sites not fully solved. Future: smaller sites, more tumour types.

heading: O4 - Clinical evaluation: performance, escalation appropriateness, workload, usability, trust and safety

papers.title: Reporting guideline for the early-stage clinical evaluation of decision support systems driven by artificial intelligence: DECIDE-AI
papers.authors: Vasey B, Nagendran M, Campbell B, Clifton DA, Collins GS, et al., McCulloch P
papers.aim: To give a reporting guideline for the first live clinical studies of AI decision support.
papers.method: International Delphi consensus with experts and stakeholders.
papers.result: Checklist of 17 AI-specific items and 10 generic items, covering human factors, safety, and user interaction.
papers.gap: Guideline only, it does not say which metrics to use for deferral.
papers.relation: Our O4 study is exactly this early stage. We should design and report it using DECIDE-AI.
papers.limitations: Needs adoption by journals. Future: updates as field changes.

papers.title: Reporting guidelines for clinical trial reports for interventions involving artificial intelligence: the CONSORT-AI extension
papers.authors: Liu X, Cruz Rivera S, Moher D, Calvert MJ, Denniston AK; SPIRIT-AI and CONSORT-AI Working Group
papers.aim: To extend CONSORT for randomised trials that test AI interventions.
papers.method: Delphi process and consensus meeting.
papers.result: 14 new items, for example describing the AI version, input data, how humans interact with the output, and error analysis.
papers.gap: For RCTs, which come after early-stage studies.
papers.relation: Our study is not an RCT, but these items help us describe AI version, input and human interaction. Useful for future trial.
papers.limitations: Not for early studies. Future: updates.

papers.title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
papers.authors: Collins GS, Moons KGM, Dhiman P, Riley RD, Beam AL, et al., Logullo P
papers.aim: To update TRIPOD for prediction models built with machine learning.
papers.method: Delphi survey and consensus meeting.
papers.result: 27-item checklist covering fairness, data, model development, evaluation and open science.
papers.gap: Covers model development and validation, not live human use.
papers.relation: Use when we report the O3 models (segmentation, classification, fusion).
papers.limitations: Reporting only. Future: wider use.
papers.pdf: Not downloaded (open access on BMJ site)

papers.title: Does the Whole Exceed its Parts? The Effect of AI Explanations on Complementary Team Performance
papers.authors: Bansal G, Wu T, Zhou J, Fok R, Nushi B, Kamar E, Ribeiro MT, Weld DS
papers.aim: To test if AI explanations help humans and AI together do better than either alone.
papers.method: User studies on text tasks with AI recommendations, with and without explanations and confidence.
papers.result: Explanations made people accept AI advice more, even when the AI was wrong. Team performance was not better than just showing confidence.
papers.gap: Non-medical tasks with crowd workers.
papers.relation: Warning for our UI: showing explanations may cause over-reliance. Calibrated confidence and deferral may matter more.
papers.limitations: Lay users, not experts. Future: domain experts.

papers.title: Human-Centered Tools for Coping with Imperfect Algorithms during Medical Decision-Making
papers.authors: Cai CJ, Reif E, Hegde N, Hipp J, Kim B, Smilkov D, Wattenberg M, Viegas F, Corrado GS, Stumpe MC, Terry M
papers.aim: To give pathologists tools to refine and control a similar-image search algorithm.
papers.method: Built refinement tools (by region, by example, by concept) for a pathology image retrieval system and tested with pathologists.
papers.result: With the tools, pathologists trusted the system more, found it more useful and felt more in control, with similar accuracy.
papers.gap: Small user study, retrieval task only.
papers.relation: Our clinician must be able to amend or reject AI outputs. This shows control tools raise trust.
papers.limitations: Small sample. Future: clinical workflow testing.

papers.title: A Human-Centered Evaluation of a Deep Learning System Deployed in Clinics for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
papers.authors: Beede E, Baylor E, Hersch F, Iurchenko A, Wilcox L, Ruamviboonsuk P, Vardoulakis LM
papers.aim: To see how an AI screening system actually worked in clinics in Thailand.
papers.method: Field observation and interviews in 11 clinics before and during deployment.
papers.result: Poor lighting, image quality and slow internet caused many images to be rejected and delays. Nurses and patients faced extra steps.
papers.tools: Deep learning DR model, qualitative field study
papers.gap: Fixing the socio-technical issues was not tested.
papers.relation: Very close to our low-resource context. Shows we must evaluate the full workflow in Sri Lankan hospitals, not only accuracy.
papers.limitations: Single country, qualitative. Future: design changes and follow-up.

papers.title: Human-computer collaboration for skin cancer recognition
papers.authors: Tschandl P, Rinner C, Apalla Z, Argenziano G, Codella N, Halpern A, et al., Kittler H
papers.aim: To test different ways of giving AI support to doctors for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.method: Large reader study comparing AI output formats (class probabilities, content-based retrieval etc.) and testing with deliberately faulty AI.
papers.result: Good AI support improved accuracy most for less experienced doctors. Faulty AI misled doctors of all experience levels.
papers.gap: Online study, not real clinic.
papers.relation: Shows the format of support matters and wrong AI is risky, so escalation is needed. Useful design for our reader study.
papers.limitations: Dermatoscopy only. Future: real-world tests.
papers.pdf: Not downloaded - get from link / library

papers.title: Automation Bias in Mammography: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence BI-RADS Suggestions on Reader Performance
papers.authors: Dratsch T, Chen X, Rezazadeh Mehrizi M, Kloeckner R, Mahringer-Kunz A, Pusken M, Baessler B, Sauer S, Maintz D, Pinto dos Santos D
papers.aim: To measure how much wrong AI suggestions affect radiologists.
papers.method: Radiologists with different experience read mammograms with AI BI-RADS suggestions, some of them wrong on purpose.
papers.result: When the AI was wrong, accuracy of all groups dropped sharply, and the less experienced readers were affected the most.
papers.gap: Simulated AI, no real model.
papers.relation: Strong reason for our conservative default: when uncertain, the system must defer and not push a wrong suggestion.
papers.limitations: Single centre, small set of cases. Future: ways to reduce bias.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence-supported screen reading versus standard double reading in the Mammography Screening with Artificial Intelligence trial (MASAI)
papers.authors: Lang K, Josefsson V, Larsson AM, Larsson S, Hogberg C, Sartor H, Hofvind S, Andersson I, Rosso A
papers.aim: To check if AI triage in breast screening is safe and reduces radiologist workload.
papers.method: Randomised trial in Sweden. AI risk score decided single vs double reading, and flagged high-risk cases.
papers.result: Cancer detection was similar or higher than standard double reading, with a large cut in screen-reading workload (about 44%).
papers.gap: Interim analysis. Interval cancer results needed later.
papers.relation: Good example of AI deciding how much human review a case gets, and of measuring workload. Similar to our escalation idea.
papers.limitations: Single country, mammography only. Future: final endpoint results.
papers.pdf: Not downloaded (Lancet, open access on site)

papers.title: Automated quantitative tumour response assessment of MRI in neuro-oncology with artificial neural networks: a multicentre, retrospective study
papers.authors: Kickingereder P, Isensee F, Tursunova I, Petersen J, Neuberger U, et al., Maier-Hein KH
papers.aim: To automate brain tumour volume measurement and response assessment from MRI.
papers.method: Deep network trained on Heidelberg data, tested on a multicentre EORTC trial data set, compared with RANO assessment.
papers.result: Automated volumetric assessment was a more reliable measure of time to progression than standard RANO, and worked across many centres.
papers.gap: Retrospective, mostly glioblastoma.
papers.relation: Brain tumour MRI clinical validation example, and supports our follow-up agent using tumour volume.
papers.limitations: Western centres. Future: prospective use.

papers.title: Explainability for artificial intelligence in healthcare: a multidisciplinary perspective
papers.authors: Amann J, Blasimme A, Vayena E, Frey D, Madai VI
papers.venue: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making
papers.aim: To look at explainability from technical, legal, medical and patient views.
papers.method: Multidisciplinary analysis (perspective paper).
papers.result: Says explainability is needed for informed consent, trust and responsibility, not only a technical feature.
papers.gap: No experiments.
papers.relation: Supports our 'transparency of basis' principle and how we explain escalation decisions to clinicians.
papers.limitations: Conceptual. Future: practical guidance.

papers.title: Real-World Integration of a Sepsis Deep Learning Technology Into Routine Clinical Care: Implementation Study
papers.authors: Sendak MP, Ratliff W, Sarro D, Alderton E, Futoma J, Gao M, Nichols M, Revoir M, Yashar F, Miller C, Kester K, Sandhu S, Corey K, Brajer N, Tan C, Lin A, Brown T, Engelbosch S, Anstrom K, Elish MC, Heller K, Donohoe R, Theiling J, Poon E, Balu S, Bedoya A, O'Brien C
papers.aim: To describe how a sepsis deep learning tool (Sepsis Watch) was put into daily use at Duke.
papers.method: Implementation study: governance, workflow design, training of rapid response nurses, monitoring.
papers.result: Tool was integrated with a clear team, workflow and governance. Lessons on clinician roles and trust.
papers.tools: Deep learning on EHR data, clinical workflow
papers.gap: Outcome effect not fully reported in this paper.
papers.relation: Gives practical lessons on governance, roles and monitoring we need for the registry deployment.
papers.limitations: One US hospital. Future: outcome studies.
papers.pdf: Not downloaded - get from link / library

papers.title: Foundations for an Empirically Determined Scale of Trust in Automated Systems
papers.authors: Jian JY, Bisantz AM, Drury CG
papers.aim: To build a questionnaire that measures human trust in automation.
papers.method: Word elicitation and rating studies, cluster analysis to form scale items.
papers.result: 12-item trust scale, still widely used in human-AI studies.
papers.gap: Not made for AI or medicine.
papers.relation: Ready tool to measure clinician trust in O4 (together with SUS for usability and NASA-TLX for workload).
papers.limitations: Old, general automation. Future: AI-specific validation.
